claim: IL-2 signals through a heterodimeric receptor formed by IL-2 receptor beta (IL-2Rβ, CD122) and common gamma chain (γc, CD132) expressed on T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and B cells.
source: Interleukin-2 (IL-2) is a classical pleiotropic cytokine that signals through a heterodimeric receptor formed by IL-2 receptor beta (IL-2Rβ, CD122) and common gamma chain (γc, CD132) expressed on T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and B cells (Hatakeyama et al., 1989; Takeshita et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hatakeyama et al., 1989; Takeshita et al., 1992) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: IL-2Rα (CD25) sensitizes cells to IL-2 signaling.
source: Cells can further enhance their sensitivity to IL-2 by expression of the non-signaling subunit, IL-2 receptor alpha (IL-2Rα, CD25) which sensitizes cells to IL-2 signaling (Cosman et al., 1984; Leonard et al., 1984; Nikaido et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Cosman et al., 1984; Leonard et al., 1984; Nikaido et al., 1984).

claim: IL-2 was originally described as a T cell stimulatory factor.
source: Although IL-2 was originally described as a T cell stimulatory factor (Morgan et al., 1976), mice deficient in IL-2 or the IL-2 receptor were found to develop severe autoimmunity (Sadlack et al., 1995; Sadlack et al., 1993; Suzuki et al., 1995; Willerford et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morgan et al., 1976.

claim: Mice deficient in IL-2 or the IL-2 receptor develop severe autoimmunity.
source: Although IL-2 was originally described as a T cell stimulatory factor (Morgan et al., 1976), mice deficient in IL-2 or the IL-2 receptor were found to develop severe autoimmunity (Sadlack et al., 1995; Sadlack et al., 1993; Suzuki et al., 1995; Willerford et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Sadlack et al., 1995; Sadlack et al., 1993; Suzuki et al., 1995; Willerford et al., 1995).

claim: IL-2 signaling is critical for maintenance of regulatory T cells (Tregs).
source: This seeming paradox was resolved by the finding that IL-2 signaling is critical for maintenance of regulatory T cells (Tregs) which play an important role in suppressing immune activation (Fontenot et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fontenot et al., 2005.

claim: Transfer of Tregs inhibits autoimmune syndrome in IL-2Rβ-deficient mice.
source: Indeed, transfer of Tregs was shown to inhibit autoimmune syndrome in IL-2Rβ-deficient mice (Malek et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Malek et al., 2002.

claim: NK cells express high levels of IL-2Rβ and respond to both IL-2 and IL-15.
source: NK cells express high levels of IL-2Rβ and respond to both IL-2 and the related cytokine, IL-15 which shares signaling receptors IL-2Rβ/γc with IL-2 (Carson et al., 1994; Giri et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carson et al., 1994 and Giri et al., 1994.

claim: Naïve T cells express low levels of IL-2 receptor components and are relatively insensitive to IL-2 stimulation until after upregulation following activation.
source: Naïve T cells express low levels of IL-2 receptor components and thus are relatively insensitive to IL-2 stimulation until after upregulation of IL-2 receptor components following activation (Au-Yeung et al., 2017; Leonard et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Au-Yeung et al., 2017 and Leonard et al., 1985.

claim: Tregs constitutively express IL-2Rα.
source: Unlike naïve T cells, Tregs constitutively express IL-2Rα (Sakaguchi et al., 1995) and are further sensitized to IL-2 by miR-155-dependent repression of suppressor of cytokine signaling 1 (SOCS1) (Lu et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sakaguchi et al., 1995.

claim: Tregs are sensitized to IL-2 by miR-155-dependent repression of SOCS1.
source: Unlike naïve T cells, Tregs constitutively express IL-2Rα (Sakaguchi et al., 1995) and are further sensitized to IL-2 by miR-155-dependent repression of suppressor of cytokine signaling 1 (SOCS1) (Lu et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lu et al., 2015 and Lu et al., 2009.

claim: Low doses of IL-2 activate Tregs without inducing signaling on naïve T cells and NK cells while high doses activate both Tregs and naïve T cells and NK cells.
source: These differences in cell type sensitivity create threshold effects where low doses of IL-2 activate Tregs without inducing signaling on naïve T cells and NK cells while high doses of IL-2 activate both Tregs as well as naïve T cells and NK cells (Grinberg-Bleyer et al., 2010; Matsuoka et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grinberg-Bleyer et al., 2010; Matsuoka et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2015.

claim: Antibodies against IL-2 that favor binding to IL-2Rα expressing cells (JES6-1) can potentiate Tregs by sterically blocking interactions between IL-2Rβ and IL-2.
source: Antibodies against IL-2 that favor binding to IL-2Rα expressing cells (JES6-1) can potentiate Tregs by sterically blocking interactions between IL-2Rβ and IL-2 (Boyman et al., 2006; Spangler et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boyman et al., 2006 and Spangler et al., 2015.

claim: IL-2 muteins with reduced affinity for IL-2Rβ increase dependence on IL-2Rα and enhance Treg selectivity.
source: Similarly, IL-2 muteins with reduced affinity for IL-2Rβ have been used to increase dependence on IL-2Rα and enhance Treg selectivity (Khoryati et al., 2020; Peterson et al., 2018; Shanafelt et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Khoryati et al., 2020; Peterson et al., 2018; Shanafelt et al., 2000.

claim: Amino acid substitution at IL-2 Q126 tunes cytokine activity.
source: (B) Amino acid substitution at IL-2 Q126 tune cytokine activity. IL-2 variants were expressed on the super-2 H9 background (L80F, R81D, L85V, I86V, I92F), an IL-2 variant with high affinity for IL-2Rβ, and assayed for dose-dependent phosphorylation of STAT5 (pSTAT5) by phosphoflow cytometry in YT cells following a 15 min stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating dose-response curves for different Q126 substitutions.

claim: Mutations in IL-2 at the γc binding interface impair receptor dimerization in the context of live cell membranes.
source: (C–E) Mutations in IL-2 at the γc binding interface impair receptor dimerization in the context of live cell membranes.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule particle tracking data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: H9-REH and H9-REK showed reduced receptor dimerization relative to H9 as measured by co-tracking of IL-2Rβ and γc.
source: As predicted, H9-REH and H9-REK showed reduced receptor dimerization relative to H9 as measured by co-tracking of IL-2Rβ and γc (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: H9-REH, H9-REK, and H9-RETR had reduced γc binding relative to H9.
source: H9-REH, H9-REK, and H9-RETR had reduced γc binding relative to H9, indicating the reduced receptor dimerization observed in cells is due to impaired interactions with γc (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: IL-2 administration reduced the frequency of T and B cells while causing an increase in the frequency of NK cells and granulocytes.
source: IL-2 administration reduced the frequency of T and B cells while causing an increase in the frequency of NK cells and granulocytes (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: IL-2-REH increased the frequency of T cells while modestly reducing B cell frequency due to expansion of T cells.
source: In contrast, IL-2-REH increased the frequency of T cells while modestly reducing B cell frequency due to expansion of T cells (Figure 2A–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: IL-2-REH dramatically increased the frequency and number of Tregs without increasing the frequency or number of IL-2Rα+ conventional CD4+ T cells.
source: IL-2 administration did not significantly impact Treg frequency or absolute number; however, IL-2-REH dramatically increased the frequency and number of Tregs without increasing the frequency or number of IL-2Rα+ conventional CD4+ T cells (Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: IL-2 decreased the frequency of naïve CD8+ T cells with an increase in effector memory T cells while IL-2-REH caused a slight increase in the frequency and number of central memory CD8+ T cells.
source: Assessment of CD8+ T cell memory populations following cytokine treatment revealed that IL-2 decreased the frequency of naïve CD8+ T cells with an increase in effector memory T cells while IL-2-REH caused a slight increase in the frequency and number of central memory CD8+ T cells (Figure 2G–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G-J and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–D.

claim: IL-2, and to a lesser extent IL-2-REH and IL-2-REK, increased the frequency of IFNγ-producing CD8+ T cells following restimulation.
source: IL-2, and to a lesser extent IL-2-REH and IL-2-REK, increased the frequency of IFNγ-producing CD8+ T cells following restimulation (Figure 2K–L, Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2K-L and Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: IL-2-REH increased the frequency of Tregs in the CD45.1 recipient compartment but not the CD45.2 donor compartment.
source: IL-2-REH increased the frequency of Tregs in the CD45.1 recipient compartment but not the CD45.2 donor, strongly suggesting that IL-2-REH acts to expand preexisting Tregs (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by adoptive transfer experiment data shown in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IL-2 and IL-2-REH resulted in a similar level of EdU incorporation in Tregs while IL-2 led to higher levels of EdU incorporation than IL-2-REH in CD8+ T cells.
source: IL-2 and IL-2-REH resulted in a similar level of EdU incorporation in Tregs while IL-2 led to higher levels of EdU incorporation than IL-2-REH in CD8+ T cells (Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 3E-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IL-2-REH induced phosphorylation of STAT5 to about 40% of the maximal level achieved by IL-2 following a 20 min stimulation in regulatory T cells.
source: In regulatory T cells, IL-2-REH induced phosphorylation of STAT5 to about 40% of the maximal level achieved by IL-2 following a 20 min stimulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphoflow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IL-2 and IL-2-REH induced very similar gene expression programs in Tregs following a 4 hr cytokine stimulation.
source: RNA-seq analysis revealed that IL-2 and IL-2-REH induced very similar gene expression programs in Tregs following a 4 hr cytokine stimulation as indicated by the small number of differentially regulated genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: IL-2 and IL-2-REH increased expression of Bcl2, Myc, Ifng, Gzmb, and Lta in Tregs.
source: IL-2 and IL-2-REH increased expression of Bcl2, Myc, Ifng, Gzmb, and Lta (Figure 4D–H)
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D-H.

claim: IL-2-REH fails to induce STAT5 phosphorylation in CD8+ T cells.
source: (I) IL-2-REH fails to induce STAT5 phosphorylation in CD8+ T cells. Dose-response (left) and histogram at 2 μM (right) of STAT5 phosphorylation in ex vivo CD8+ T cells following a 20 min cytokine stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphoflow cytometry data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: IL-2 but not IL-2-REH resulted in upregulation of Bcl2, Myc, Ifng, Gzmb, and Lta in CD8+ T cells.
source: These transcriptional changes were confirmed by qPCR where IL-2 but not IL-2-REH resulted in upregulation of Bcl2, Myc, Ifng, Gzmb, and Lta (Figure 4L–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4L-P.

claim: IL-2-REH and IL-2-REK responsiveness positively correlated with expression of IL-2Rα and γc but not IL-2Rβ.
source: IL-2-REH and IL-2-REK responsiveness positively correlated with expression of IL-2Rα and γc but not IL-2Rβ, indicating that expression of IL-2Rα and γc may contribute to the selectivity of IL-2 partial agonists (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Increased affinity for IL-2Rβ (H9-REH) attenuated the IL-2-REH-mediated increase in Treg frequency.
source: Increased affinity for IL-2Rβ (H9-REH) attenuated the IL-2-REH-mediated increase in Treg frequency, indicating that IL-2Rα dependence is important for cell type selectivity of IL-2-REH in vivo (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experiment data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Co-culture in IL-2-REH produced an enrichment in IL-2Rα-expressing cells suggesting knockout cells were reduced in their capacity to respond to IL-2-REH.
source: When cultured in IL-2, cells remained roughly at their input ratios, suggesting a negligible contribution of IL-2Rα expression. In contrast, co-culture in IL-2-REH produced an enrichment in IL-2Rα-expressing cells suggesting knockout cells were reduced in their capacity to respond to IL-2-REH (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-culture experiment data shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: Overexpression of SOCS1 impaired phosphorylation of STAT5 in response to IL-2-REH but not IL-2.
source: Overexpression of SOCS1 impaired phosphorylation of STAT5 in response to IL-2-REH but not IL-2, suggesting that the IL-2-REH signaling is more sensitive to negative regulation by SOCS1 (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphoflow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: Tregs from cytokine-treated mice were capable of suppressing proliferation of conventional CD4+ T cells at similar ratios.
source: Tregs from cytokine-treated mice were capable of suppressing proliferation of conventional CD4+ T cells (Tcon) at similar ratios, indicating that IL-2-REH-induced proliferation does not impair the suppressive capacity of expanded Tregs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro suppression assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: IL-2-REH improved recovery from DSS-induced colitis as measured by body weight on day 16.
source: All mice lost weight as a result of DSS administration; however, IL-2-REH improved recovery as measured by body weight on day 16 (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: H&E staining of distal colon sections showed elevated disease score following DSS induction, an effect which was attenuated in mice receiving IL-2-REH but not IL-2 or IL-2-N88D.
source: Consistent with these findings, hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) staining of distal colon sections showed elevated disease score following DSS induction, an effect which was attenuated in mice receiving IL-2-REH but not IL-2 or IL-2-N88D (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: IL-2-REH increased Treg frequency in the mesenteric lymph nodes in the context of DSS-induced colitis.
source: The mitigating effects of IL-2-REH administration on weight loss and disease score were accompanied by increased Treg frequency in the mesenteric lymph nodes, indicating that IL-2-REH expansion of Tregs is maintained in the context of an inflammatory response (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: IL-2 but not IL-2-REH or IL-2-N88D increased NK cell frequency in the mesenteric lymph node during DSS-induced colitis.
source: Importantly, DSS induction did not alter IL-2-REH specificity as IL-2 but not IL-2-REH or IL-2-N88D increased NK cell frequency in the mesenteric lymph node (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: DSS administration enhanced Treg infiltration in the colon.
source: While disease induction did not impact Treg frequency in mesenteric lymph nodes, DSS administration enhanced Treg infiltration in the colon, an effect that was not significantly impacted by cytokine treatment (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Treatment with IL-2, IL-2-REH, or IL-2-N88D increased the presence of GzmB+Foxp3+ cells in the colon.
source: Treatment with IL-2, IL-2-REH, or, IL-2-N88D increased the presence GzmB+Foxp3+ cells, suggesting that all of these cytokines were capable of promoting Treg activation in the tissue (Figure 6H)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: IL-2 signaling is initiated when IL-2 first binds to IL-2Rβ, following recruitment of γc, which results in trans-phosphorylation of JAK1/JAK3, and activation of STAT5 and other pathway components.
source: IL-2 signaling is initiated when IL-2 first binds to IL-2Rβ, following recruitment of γc, which results in trans-phosphorylation of JAK1/JAK3, and activation of STAT5 and other pathway components.
evidence: This is a description of the IL-2 signaling mechanism based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The mutational strategy of targeting IL-2 residues that contact γc has the advantage of capping maximal signaling (Emax) by weakening the recruitment of γc.
source: This mutational strategy has the advantage of capping maximal signaling (Emax) by weakening the recruitment of γc, the final step of IL-2 receptor assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the design strategy and the known mechanism of IL-2 receptor assembly.

claim: IL-2 and IL-15 share signaling receptors IL-2Rβ and γc.
source: NK cells express high levels of IL-2Rβ and respond to both IL-2 and the related cytokine, IL-15 which shares signaling receptors IL-2Rβ/γc with IL-2 (Carson et al., 1994; Giri et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carson et al., 1994 and Giri et al., 1994.

claim: IL-2 acts as a central regulator of immunity by supporting both pro- and anti-inflammatory responses.
source: Thus, IL-2 acts as a central regulator of immunity by supporting both pro- and anti-inflammatory responses.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the preceding discussion of IL-2's dual roles.

claim: IL-15 promotes induction of a 'central memory' phenotype characterized by expression of both CD44 and CD62L.
source: In contrast, IL-15, which shares IL-2Rβ/γc signaling receptors with IL-2, promotes induction of a 'central memory' phenotype characterized by expression of both CD44 and CD62L.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about IL-15's effects on T cell memory differentiation.

claim: Central memory CD8+ T cells have improved persistence and antitumor effects in the context of adoptive cell therapy.
source: Central memory CD8+ T cells have improved persistence and antitumor effects in the context of adoptive cell therapy (Klebanoff et al., 2005; Manjunath et al., 2001; Wherry et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Klebanoff et al., 2005; Manjunath et al., 2001; Wherry et al., 2003.

claim: Granzyme B (GzmB) has been implicated in the suppressive activity of Tregs through killing of antigen presenting cells.
source: Previously, the cytotoxic effector molecule, granzyme B (GzmB) has been implicated in the suppressive activity of Tregs through killing of antigen presenting cells (Cao et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cao et al., 2007.

claim: Tregs are able to suppress T cell-mediated colitis.
source: An early demonstration of the suppressive capacity of regulatory T cells was provided by adoptive transfer experiments showing that Tregs are able to suppress T cell-mediated colitis (Read et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Read et al., 2000.

claim: IL-2Rα+Tregs are essential for suppression of colitis induced by transfer of CD45RBhi cells.
source: In this model, colitis is induced by transfer of naïve CD45RBhi cells into immunodeficient mice and can be prevented by co-transfer of CD45RBlo cells of which IL-2Rα+Tregs are essential (Ostanin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ostanin et al., 2009.

claim: IL-2-REH was able to expand Tregs in the T cell transfer colitis model.
source: Interestingly, this was not due to an inability of IL-2-REH to expand Tregs as elevated Treg frequency was observed in cytokine-treated mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: IL-2-REH was able to stimulate Tregs as measured by expression of activation markers IL-2Rα, GzmB, and ICOS in the T cell transfer colitis model.
source: Similarly, IL-2-REH was able to stimulate Tregs as measured by expression of activation markers IL-2Rα, GzmB, and ICOS (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-F.

claim: Cytokine receptor signaling depends largely on receptor dimerization.
source: Unlike GPCR which undergo ligand-induced confirmational changes, cytokine receptor signaling depends largely on receptor dimerization (Engelowski et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Engelowski et al., 2018 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Modulating the affinity of IL-2 for its receptor can shift the monomer-dimer equilibrium and promote distinct levels of intracellular signaling.
source: We find that modulating the affinity of IL-2 for its receptor can shift the monomer-dimer equilibrium and promote distinct levels of intracellular signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IL-2 muteins which fail to signal on one cell population act as full or partial agonists on others.
source: Importantly, these effects are highly dependent on expression of receptor subunits such that IL-2 muteins which fail to signal on one cell population act as full or partial agonists on others (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The affinity of IL-2 for IL-2Rβ predominantly impacts the dose sensitivity of cytokine signaling rather than the maximal response.
source: The affinity of IL-2 for IL-2Rβ predominantly impacts the dose sensitivity of cytokine signaling rather than the maximal response such increased cytokine concentration can compensate for reduced IL-2Rβ affinity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and comparison with previous approaches.

claim: IL-2 and IL-15 exhibit very similar signaling on CD8+ T cells in vitro.
source: Indeed, IL-2 shares signaling receptors IL-2Rβ and γc with IL-15 (Carson et al., 1994; Giri et al., 1994). Despite exhibiting very similar signaling on CD8+ T cells in vitro (Ring et al., 2012), IL-2 and IL-15 have many divergent biological functions in vivo (Lodolce et al., 1998; Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ring et al., 2012.

claim: IL-2 and IL-15 have many divergent biological functions in vivo.
source: Despite exhibiting very similar signaling on CD8+ T cells in vitro (Ring et al., 2012), IL-2 and IL-15 have many divergent biological functions in vivo (Lodolce et al., 1998; Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lodolce et al., 1998 and Ma et al., 2006.

claim: Differences in IL-2 and IL-15 have been attributed to unique receptors, IL-2Rα and IL-15Rα, which play important roles in determining cell type specificity of cytokine signaling.
source: Differences in IL-2 and IL-15 have been attributed to unique receptors, IL-2Rα and IL-15Rα, which play important roles in determining cell type specificity of cytokine signaling (Waldmann, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Waldmann, 2006.

claim: Type I interferons play nonredundant roles in antiviral immunity by modulating the strength of receptor dimerization.
source: This mechanism of functional diversification through altered receptor dimerization shares some features with type I interferons (IFNs), a large class of cytokines that signal though receptors IFNAR1 and IFNAR2. Despite the use of a shared receptor complex, type I IFNs play nonredundant roles in antiviral immunity by modulating the strength of receptor dimerization (Ng et al., 2016; Ng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ng et al., 2016 and Ng et al., 2015.

claim: IL-2 and IL-15 are the only natural ligands of the IL-2Rβ/γc receptor complex.
source: While IL-2 and IL-15 are the only natural ligands of the IL-2Rβ/γc receptor complex, we show here that additional IL-2 receptor agonists with divergent biological behavior can be generated by systematically altering receptor binding.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Additional IL-2 receptor agonists with divergent biological behavior can be generated by systematically altering receptor binding.
source: While IL-2 and IL-15 are the only natural ligands of the IL-2Rβ/γc receptor complex, we show here that additional IL-2 receptor agonists with divergent biological behavior can be generated by systematically altering receptor binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental work presented in the manuscript.

claim: The approach of using partial agonists to exploit intrinsic differences in cytokine sensitivity may be generally applicable to other pleiotropic cytokines.
source: As many cytokines use differences in receptor expression and signaling pathway components to achieve cell type selectivity, this approach may be more generally applicable to other pleiotropic cytokines.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential generalizability of the approach.
